---
title: "Taming Wilderness"
author: "DK"
date: "2026-08-10"
categories: [convenience, needs]
---

It is estimated that a country in East Asia has one shrine or temple for every 800 people, compared to about one convenience store for every 2,200.

In a city, that was nation's capital for over 1,000 years, there are roughly 2,500 temples and shrines—about four to five times as many as its 500 to 600 convenience stores.

Nationwide, the country boasts about 157,000 temples and shrines compared to roughly 57,000 convenience stores—a ratio of nearly three to one.

No matter which figures are used for comparison, this country has an abundance of both sacred spaces and convenience stores, ready to meet both the spiritual and physical needs of its people.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

When traveling abroad, I rarely expect to be invited into someone’s personal home.

In fact, outside of Korea and the United States—my original home and my secondary one—I can count on one hand the number of times I have stepped inside a local's residence.

While I have shared many meals with locals, these gatherings almost always take place in public venues rather than private living quarters.

It is an understandable dynamic.

People are busy, urban homes in many parts of the world are compact, and public spaces naturally serve as the ideal stage for entertaining guests.

In dense, modern landscapes, daily life shifts outward.

Public venues have become the communal living rooms of society.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

My parents, on the other hand, almost always opened our home to visitors—many of whom were mere acquaintances when they first arrived.

They never owned a spacious home.

Their living room and dining area held only a simple sofa and a small table, and their kitchen was roughly the size of a modern-day pantry.

Yet they constantly invited, fed, and entertained guests, regardless of how well they knew them.

In doing so, they honored the counsel found in the letters to Timothy, continuing a long-standing tradition of Christian hospitality.

Convenience was not a factor in their decision-making.

Instead, by opening their doors and serving others, they met both the emotional and physical needs of their guests—elevating simple, everyday meals into moments of spiritual connection.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

I have wondered how many of our essential traditions and practices have been outsourced and offloaded in the name of convenience.

Not long ago, the home was the primary educational, vocational, and spiritual center of daily life.

One modern-day religious leader observed:

> "In contrast, in today’s urban society, few members experience consistent family-centered activities. Urban living, modern transportation, organized entertainment, and high-speed communication have made it easy for youth to treat their homes as boardinghouses—places where they sleep and take an occasional meal, but where there is far less parental direction of their activities."

It is time to say no to drive-through-style solutions that offer instant satisfaction, whether physical, emotional, or spiritual.

Instead, we must work to rebuild the home as a sanctuary where principles are practiced and individuals are refined.

The leader continued:

> "In times past, one of the great influences that unified families was the experience of struggling together in pursuit of a common goal—such as taming the wilderness or earning a living. The family was an organized unit of economic production. Today, most families are units of economic consumption, requiring far less organization and cooperation."

We will continue to honor and visit sacred monuments dedicated to our spiritual well-being, like ancient shrines and temples.

And we will continue to utilize modern convenience stores that fulfill immediate daily needs.

But if convenience becomes the main deciding factor, we lose something vital.

We would do well to look back a generation or two to remember how our progenitors tamed the wilderness—and, in doing so, tamed the natural man within.

That taming of the environment and of oneself is life’s true adventure—the very thing society subtly and conveniently tries to replace.
